I head to the Woolmark for supper and a room for the night.

Over breakfast I lean toward the clerk watching the door. "Trouble with a wagon? I've handled mired carts before — is there work or reward in it for someone who can chase it down?"
"A silver for a day's walking and plain facts — done. I'll take the mill road and come back to you with what I find."

"Agreed — four silver, one in hand. I'll take the road now and come back with an answer, one way or the other." I pocket the silver and head for the quarry at a good pace.

140.prose:
The pitch caught on the second strike of the flint and the torch took with a fat yellow flare, throwing his own shadow huge up the quarry face behind him. He kept to the left wall, where old rail-iron ran rusted into the stone, and went in a few steps at a time, stopping each time to let the sound of the cut come back to him.

The grinding. The mutter. Closer now, and the smell of blood stronger, mixed with the sour reek of something animal and unwashed.

The mouth narrowed where a fall of rubble had half-blocked it years ago, and he edged around the shoulder of it, torch held out ahead of the staff — and the cut opened below him.

It was a bowl, maybe forty yards across, terraced down in old working levels, and the light of his torch reached only the first of them. But the first level held enough. Sacks, a dozen or more, torn open, grain scattered and trampled into a reeking paste. A horse lying on its side, legs stiff, the saddle-cut still dark on its flank. And against the far wall of that level, huddled into a niche in the rock with his hands bound before him with what looked like rein-leather, a heavyset man in a carter's smears of flour and blood — Brast, or what was left of him: one eye swollen shut, and the muttering coming from his lips without pause, a man talking to himself because there was no one else.

Between Brast and the light, stretched full-length among the ruined sacks with its head down in a torn one, lay the thing that had dragged him there.

Bigger than a hound, longer, low-slung on four legs — and the forefeet were wrong, splayed and grasping, three toes each with claws the torchlight found and turned orange. Its hide was grey as quarry stone. It fed without hurry, and its tail, thick as his arm, moved slow and satisfied through the spilled grain.

The grinding he'd heard from the road, he understood now, was the sound of it dragging a sack.

It had not lifted its head.

144.prose:
The terraces took him down in three drops, torch in one hand, and the beast's smell got worse as he came level with it — burnt hide and grain gone to rot and the sweetish reek off the horse. It did not move. He kept the staff between it and himself anyway until he was past.

Brast watched him the whole way down, his breath coming quick and shallow.

"Careful — the other one, there was a second one, smaller—" His voice pitched up as Alaric came close, hands coming up bound together. "It went off. Before dawn. I don't know where it went."

The cut came down between the rein-leather and the swelling on his wrists, and the bindings fell. Brast worked his hands apart with a groan, the skin beneath striped raw and the fingers slow to answer him.

"Two days," he said, mostly to himself. "Or three. I stopped counting when the light got bad."

Alaric checked him over by torchlight. The scalp wound had crusted thick and broken open again at least once, the hair matted stiff with it; the eye below it was swollen but the man could squint through the lid of the other well enough. His ribs were bruised — he hissed when the fingers probed there, said it was the dragging, it had hauled him by the collar of his coat up the drag-path like a pup — and his wrists were the worst of the fresh damage. He was filthy, dehydrated, shaky in the arms and legs. Nothing that said he would not walk.

"There's a second one," he said again, watching Alaric's face. "Smaller. That's the one that took the horses — no, it went for the grain first, they both did, and the big one dragged me up here after I ran for the cut." He looked past Alaric, up at the beast on the floor, and his jaw worked. "Is it the pelt they'll want? The Guild? I heard Ovell say—"

He stopped, and a shiver went through him that had nothing to do with the cold of the stone.

"Water. Please. Have you got water?"

148.prose:
They went up the wall-side path in single file, Alaric first with the torch held high and away from the rock so it threw its light wide, Brast behind him with one hand trailing the stone. The grain crunched under their boots no matter how carefully they set them down, and each crunch sounded enormous in the cut, and each time Brast stopped breathing until Alaric moved on again.

Halfway up, Brast whispered, "The drag-path comes in from the west side. If the small one uses it, it'll come from your left at the top. Worth knowing."

It was worth knowing. Alaric kept his head turned to the left the rest of the climb.

The terraces gave them the last of the rubble, then the slope of spilled sacks, then the raw grey light of midday at the quarry mouth, flat and colourless after the torch. Brast squinted at it and swore softly, pleased.

The wagon stood where the engine of the story had left it, twenty paces off the road, one wheel still canted, the harness cut and dangling. Beyond it the mill road ran pale and empty in both directions. No second beast on the road, none among the sacks, none on the drag-path that they could see. The wind came down the cut at their backs and carried the burnt smell out over the fields, which was its own kind of warning — anything downwind would know where they had been.

Brast leaned against the quarry mouth with his bound-hands callus catching on the stone, breathing hard from the climb, and looked at the wagon.

"I can walk to the city," he said. "Slow, but I can. Or you go ahead and tell them, and I sit in the wagon till someone comes. Ovell'll pay for the wagon to be fetched, won't he — it's his grain still in it, half of it. Someone will want that back." He rubbed his raw wrists, wincing. "Your call, Master Mage. You found me. You're the one that knows the road."

150.prose:
Brast took the arm with a grip still clumsy in his damaged fingers, and they came up out of the quarry cut onto the mill road together, the smaller man's weight coming and going on Alaric's shoulder as his legs tired and recovered.

The road ran pale and quiet eastward. A kestrel worked the hedgerow ahead of them for a while and moved off. Once Brast stopped dead at a rustle in the verge, and it was only a wind-drifted sack-end caught on a thorn, and he laughed at himself — a short, rough laugh — and they went on.

He talked most of the way, at first in bursts and then steadier, the way men do when the fear is still draining out of them. About the wagon, the grain, how Ovell counted every sack twice and would count them twice again. About his father, who had driven this same mill road for nineteen years and never once lost so much as a wheel-rim. About how he had run for the cut when the big one came, and how that had saved him and doomed him in the same breath.

"You'll tell it plain to Ovell," he said, somewhere past the halfway mile. "That I ran. Don't dress it up. He'll dock me for the horses either way, and I'd rather he heard it true from a Mage than false from me."

They walked through the early afternoon with the sun thin behind the cloud, and the city showed itself before long — walls first, then rooftops, then smoke standing up from the kiln district. The west gate had its usual afternoon traffic: carts in, a drover's sheep bawling, a gate-guard who looked twice at the state of Brast and decided it was no business of the watch.

Inside, Brast slowed at the first turning.

"Mill yard's this way, past the shrine," he said. "Ovell keeps to the yard after midday. Or the Guild hall's down by the fountain, if you'd rather make your report first." He stopped, one hand on the wall, and looked at Alaric. "Either way, I'm for home after. My mother's going to weep all over me and I'll let her."

152.prose:
The mill yard announced itself before they reached it: the thump and sigh of the wheel, the sweet dust smell of cut grain, sacks stacked under an awning with a boy counting them and losing count and starting again. Brast turned in at the gate with his chin up, and the boy dropped his tally-stick.

"Mother's at the house," Brast said, not stopping. "Tell her after. If I sit down I won't get up."

Ovell was where Brast had said he'd be, in the yard office with its door open to the noise, a round man bent over a ledger, ink to the second knuckle. He looked up at footsteps, saw the staff and the robes, and stood so fast his stool went over behind him.

"You found him. Where—" and then Brast filled the doorway behind Alaric, and Ovell came around the desk and took the carter's son by both shoulders and looked him over — the wrists, the flour, the dried blood — and said nothing for a moment.

"I'm whole," Brast said. "Mostly. Ran, Ovell. Left the wagon. You'll hear it true from him or not at all, so hear it now." And he stood there while Alaric gave it plain: both horses taken, one beast dead in the quarry cut, a second smaller one still loose somewhere near the drag-path, the wagon twenty paces off the roadside with half the grain intact.

Ovell heard it all with his hands flat on the desk, and when it was done he sat down heavily and rubbed his face.

"Half the grain. Half." He said it the way another man would say a prayer of thanks. "The college will want the rest of the order and an account of this, but that's mine to manage." He looked up at Alaric, and the ink-stained hand went to a drawer, and he was already counting before he finished speaking. "You went back out when my own men wouldn't. You brought him walking in on his own legs. Both jobs, the finding and the bringing — name what's fair, and if it's fair I'll pay it standing up."

154.prose:
"Two silver." Ovell said it as if testing the weight, and then nodded once and counted it out onto the desk — two coins, then two more copper set apart — and stopped himself. "No. Two silver, you said, both jobs. That's what's fair." He pushed the two silver across. "The copper's Brast's notion if you ask him, not mine."

Brast, leaning in the doorway, grinned for the first time since the quarry. "It's robbery, Ovell. Take it."

Ovell took it, in his own fashion: he wrote two silver in the ledger with a steady hand this time, blotted it, and closed the book. Then he was up and moving, the roundness of him suddenly purposeful, calling across the yard. "Tam! Leave the counting! Take four men and the spare team out the west gate — wagon twenty paces off the road by the old quarry, one wheel canted. Load what grain's whole and leave the torn. And you go round by the road, not the cut, and if anything with three toes shows itself, you leave it be and come home. Understand? Leave it be!"

The boy was already running for the stable side.

Ovell came back to the desk and stood with his fists on the ledger, and some of the stiffness went out of his shoulders all at once.

"The college will hear it was a Mage who brought my carter's son home," he said. "That's worth more than the grain, in this city, if you're minded to work for factors and their like. We get beasts on the roads. We get thieves. We get letters that need carrying and cellars that need walking." He rubbed his ink-stained cuffs absently. "But you've a Guild plate on you already, so I expect you know that better than I do."

Brast pushed off the doorway. "I'm for home," he said, to Alaric more than to Ovell. "You told it plain, Master Mage. I'll not forget it." And he was gone past the shrine before Ovell could start on him about the horses.

Ovell watched him go, then looked back at Alaric, and there was a ledger-open kind of patience in the look, as if he had more to say if Alaric were staying to hear it.

176.prose:
He stepped over the beast's hind leg, boots careful on the blood-slick bench, and the overhang's shadow took him. Cool air, damp stone, the smell of grain and something sour underneath. The pale shape resolved as he came to it: not a boulder.

A man lay on his back against the recess wall, one leg swollen thick below the knee and pinned under a fallen slab of quarry stone, a torn grain sack bunched beneath his head for a pillow. A second sack, half dragged, lay across his shins. His face was gray-white with dust and days of pain, beard stubbled, eyes closed — but his chest moved, slow and shallow, and as Alaric's boots stopped beside him the eyelids fluttered and half opened.

"Mm — no. No more grain," the man mumbled, tongue thick. "You've had... enough of it..." Then his eyes found Alaric properly, and focus came into them with visible effort. He stared.

"You're not the beast." A dry, cracked laugh that turned into a cough. "College? You're from the college? Blessed saints, boy." His hand crawled off his belly and patted the air weakly. "Brast. Carter. Third day under this stone. Water — if you've got water. And don't... don't kick that slab none."

The slab sat solid across his leg, one end bedded in the floor, the other propped on a scatter of rubble. It would take a bar, a rope, or two strong backs to shift it. Behind Alaric, out in the light, the dead beast cooled and the flies worked at it, and the dragged-sack trail ran from the man's pinned leg to the empty terrace and back.

196.prose:
"Quiet it is." Joss left the cart at the quarry mouth with the reins tied short and the torch lit, and took the shovel for a carrying board. "I'll come down with you — one man carrying a stretcher is a fool, two is a stretcher."

The path along the wall was loose scree and shale, and Alaric kept to it slow, torch held low to kill the glow over the rim. Below, the cut opened into a bowl of fallen stone, and Brast's voice came up clearer with every step — still counting days to himself, still talking through slings and knots, the words running together and starting over.

Then the torchlight found him, and the talking stopped.

Brast Wenlock lay wedged between a slab the size of a hay wagon and the cut wall, one leg pinned to the knee under the stone's near edge, his own coat wadded beneath his shoulder blades for a pillow. Three days of quarry dust on him, a clay jug turned over at his hip, and his eyes went from the torch to Alaric to Joss behind and came back wet and quick.

"The boy came back." His voice cracked on it. "Told you he would. Joss Hale, you old mule, get this off me before my foot goes black."

"Alive and rude. It's him." Joss got his shoulder under the edge of the slab anyway, testing. "It's not moving, Brast. It's not moving, and it's not coming off, so we're going to lever the leg out from under it and it's going to hurt, and that's the whole of my good news."

Working together, they wedged the shovel handle under the near edge and Alaric leaned his weight on the bar until the stone gave a whisper of a gap and Brast howled through his teeth and Joss hauled the leg clear — boot crushed flat at the toe, the leg below the knee swollen twice its width and ugly, but whole.

They got him onto the shovel boards and the coat, two men lifting three days of hungry man, and started up the scree.

Halfway up, Brast stopped panting long enough to speak into Alaric's ear.

"Lad. Lad, listen." His grip tightened on Alaric's collar. "It comes at night. It comes and it takes the grain, and it checks its cache, and the last two nights it checked while I was lying here, close, so close I heard its breath. That's why it's not eaten me — I'm under its stone, near its stores. You're carrying me out of its larder with its supper in your sack, and it's in those pines."
